source.title: Regularity of maximal operators: recent progress and some open problems

accepted.question_text: Let M be the centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on R^d, defined by M f(x) = sup_{r>0} |B(x,r)|^{-1} integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, where B(x,r) is the open ball centered at x with radius r. Let the uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator be defined analogously, except that the supremum is over open balls that contain x and need not be centered at x. For f in W^{1,1}(R^d), is M f weakly differentiable and is the map f -> |grad M f| bounded from W^{1,1}(R^d) to L^1(R^d), equivalently with ||grad M f||_{L^1(R^d)} controlled by C(d)||grad f||_{L^1(R^d)}? Does the same endpoint Sobolev bound hold for the uncentered maximal operator?

For a real-valued function f on R of bounded variation, let M be the one-dimensional centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator. Must the sharp variation inequality Var(M f) <= Var(f) hold? If that exact inequality is false or out of reach, can Kurka's known constant 240004 in the inequality Var(M f) <= 240004 Var(f) be substantially improved?

For alpha >= 0, define the one-dimensional non-tangential maximal operator M_alpha by M_alpha f(x) = sup (2t)^{-1} integral_{y-t}^{y+t} |f(s)| ds over pairs (y,t) with t>0 and |x-y| <= alpha t. This interpolates between the centered operator M_0 and the uncentered operator M_1. For functions f: R -> R of bounded variation, does Var(M_alpha f) <= Var(f) hold for every 0 <= alpha < 1/3? More generally, what is the smallest alpha for which this sharp variation inequality holds?

For radial functions f in W^{1,1}(R^d), Luiro proved that the uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal function is weakly differentiable and satisfies ||grad M_tilde f||_{L^1(R^d)} <= C(d)||grad f||_{L^1(R^d)}. Does the same endpoint W^{1,1} to L^1 gradient bound hold for the centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator M acting on radial functions?

Let M_S be the spherical maximal operator on R^d, defined by taking the supremum over r>0 of the average of |f| on the sphere S^{d-1}(x,r). For dimensions d >= 2, is M_S bounded from W^{1,p}(R^d) to W^{1,p}(R^d) for the full range 1 < p <= d/(d-1)?

Let phi: R^d -> R be a nonnegative integrable convolution kernel with integral 1, let phi_t(x) = t^{-d} phi(x/t), and define M_phi f(x) = sup_{t>0} (phi_t * |f|)(x). For a real-valued function f on R of bounded variation, can one prove Var(M_phi f) <= C(phi) Var(f)? For which kernels phi can one prove the sharp version with C(phi)=1?

For 0 <= beta < d, define the centered Hardy-Littlewood fractional maximal operator by M_beta f(x) = sup_{r>0} |B(x,r)|^{beta/d - 1} integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, and define the uncentered version by taking the supremum over balls that contain x. When 0 <= beta < 1 and q = d/(d-beta), is the map f -> |grad M_beta f| bounded from W^{1,1}(R^d) to L^q(R^d)? Does the same endpoint fractional Sobolev bound hold for the uncentered fractional maximal operator?

For 0 < beta < 1 and q = d/(d-beta), a known radial result gives weak differentiability and the bound ||grad M_tilde_beta f||_{L^q(R^d)} <= C(d,beta)||grad f||_{L^1(R^d)} for radial f in W^{1,1}(R^d), where M_tilde_beta is the uncentered fractional maximal operator. Does the same statement hold for the centered fractional maximal operator M_beta acting on radial functions?

For a sequence f: Z -> R, define the discrete centered one-dimensional Hardy-Littlewood maximal function by M f(n) = sup_{r>=0} (2r+1)^{-1} sum_{k=-r}^{r} |f(n+k)|, where r ranges over nonnegative integers. If f has bounded variation on Z, must the sharp inequality Var(M f) <= Var(f) hold? If not, can Temur's known constant 294912004 in Var(M f) <= 294912004 Var(f) be substantially improved?

For 0 < beta < 1, define the one-dimensional discrete centered fractional maximal operator by M_beta f(n) = sup_{r>=0} (2r+1)^{beta-1} sum_{k=-r}^{r} |f(n+k)|, where r ranges over nonnegative integers. Let q = 1/(1-beta), and for a sequence g define Var_q(g) = (sum_{n in Z} |g(n+1)-g(n)|^q)^{1/q}. If f: Z -> R has bounded variation and M_beta f is not identically infinite, is there a universal constant C such that Var_q(M_beta f) <= C Var(f)?

Let Omega be a bounded open convex subset of R^d with Lipschitz boundary and 0 in its interior. For r>0 write Omega(x,r) = {y in R^d: r^{-1}(y-x) is in Omega}, set Omega(x,0)={x}, and let N(x,r) count lattice points in Omega(x,r). For 0 <= beta < d and f: Z^d -> R, define M_{Omega,beta} f(n) = sup_{r>=0} N(0,r)^{beta/d - 1} sum_{m in Omega(0,r)} |f(n+m)|. When 0 <= beta < 1 and q = d/(d-beta), does ||grad M_{Omega,beta} f||_{ell^q(Z^d)} <= C(d,Omega,beta)||grad f||_{ell^1(Z^d)} hold for every discrete function f? More generally, for every 0 <= alpha <= beta and q = d/(d-beta+alpha), does ||grad M_{Omega,beta} f||_{ell^q(Z^d)} <= C ||grad f||_{ell^1(Z^d)}^{1-alpha} ||f||_{ell^1(Z^d)}^{alpha} hold? Do the analogous statements hold for the uncentered Omega-fractional maximal operator?

Let M be the one-dimensional centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator. Is the derivative map f -> (M f)' continuous from W^{1,1}(R) to L^1(R)? Equivalently, whenever f_j converges to f in W^{1,1}(R), must (M f_j)' converge to (M f)' in L^1(R)?

Let M_tilde be the one-dimensional uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator. Let BV(R) be the Banach space of real-valued functions on R of bounded total variation with norm ||f||_{BV(R)} = |f(-infinity)| + Var(f), where f(-infinity) is the limit of f(x) as x tends to -infinity. Is the map M_tilde: BV(R) -> BV(R) continuous?

Let M be the one-dimensional centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator. Let BV(R) be the Banach space of real-valued functions on R of bounded total variation with norm ||f||_{BV(R)} = |f(-infinity)| + Var(f), where f(-infinity) is the limit of f(x) as x tends to -infinity. Is the map M: BV(R) -> BV(R) continuous?

For 0 < beta < 1, let M_beta be the one-dimensional centered fractional maximal operator M_beta f(x) = sup_{r>0} |B(x,r)|^{beta-1} integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, and let q = 1/(1-beta). Is the derivative map f -> (M_beta f)' both bounded and continuous from W^{1,1}(R) to L^q(R)?
